case_name: Parvathi Nairthi (Dead) Thr. LRs & Ors. v. Laxmi Nairthy (Dead) Thr. LRs & Ors.
holding_summary: A testator had bequeathed his properties to his sister under an unregistered Will, excluding his wife and children entirely, and the beneficiaries under the Will were challenged by the natural heirs who argued the exclusion itself was a suspicious circumstance. A Bench of Justices Vijay Bishnoi and Ujjal Bhuyan upheld the Will, holding that a testamentary disposition exists precisely to interfere with the ordinary line of succession, so deprivation of natural heirs does not, by itself, amount to a suspicious circumstance capable of invalidating a Will. The Court reiterated that a Will need not be registered to be valid, and that proof of a Will does not require mathematical accuracy — only that it was validly executed and attested in accordance with Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 and Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act.
why_it_matters: Natural heirs challenging a Will cannot rely merely on the fact that they were excluded or that a distant or non-family beneficiary was preferred — they must point to genuine, specific suspicious circumstances (such as an unusual signature, undue haste, or the propounder's active role in the execution), giving testators real confidence that a validly executed Will excluding even a spouse and children will be upheld.

case_name: B.S. Lalitha & Ors. v. Bhuvanesh & Ors.
holding_summary: Ruling on whether Section 6(5) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 — as substituted by the 2005 Amendment — operates as a jurisdictional bar to filing a partition suit wherever a prior partition is alleged, a Bench of Justices Augustine George Masih and Sanjay Karol held that Section 6(5) is only a narrow saving clause protecting genuine, already-completed partitions, not a threshold bar to the suit itself. The Court held that whether an alleged prior partition deed is in fact valid and binding is a question of fact for trial, and a plaint seeking partition cannot be rejected at the threshold merely because the defendants assert an earlier partition occurred.
why_it_matters: An heir seeking partition of ancestral property cannot have their suit thrown out at the first hearing merely because the other side claims an earlier family partition already happened — that claim must be proved at trial like any other disputed fact, giving genuine partition-seekers a real day in court rather than a threshold dismissal.

case_name: Chaturbhuj Pradhan v. Amar Pradhan & Anr.
holding_summary: In a dispute over a daughter's share in ancestral coparcenary property, the Supreme Court clarified the interplay between the 2005 Amendment's grant of coparcenary-by-birth status to daughters and their independent inheritance rights as Class I heirs under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. The Court held that the 2005 Amendment, which made daughters coparceners in the same manner as sons, did not take away or limit a daughter's separate, pre-existing entitlement to inherit as a Class I heir — the two routes to a daughter's share operate alongside each other rather than one displacing the other.
why_it_matters: Daughters and their advisors now have clearer Supreme Court authority that a daughter's coparcenary-by-birth right under the 2005 Amendment is additional to, not a substitute for, her separate statutory inheritance rights as a Class I heir — relevant wherever a family partition or estate distribution tries to shortchange a daughter's share by treating only one of these routes as applicable.

case_name: Deepesh Maheswari v. Renu Maheswari & Ors.
holding_summary: After a Madhya Pradesh Central Electricity Distribution Company lineman died in 2011 leaving retiral benefits, his daughters obtained an ex parte succession certificate under Section 372 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 on the footing that their mother had predeceased him, without a minor legal heir being given any real opportunity to contest the proceedings. The Supreme Court allowed the minor's appeal, quashed the succession certificate, and restored the matter to the trial court for fresh disposal within a year, holding that a minor cannot be expected to protect their inheritance rights without proper legal representation and a genuine opportunity to be heard.
why_it_matters: A succession certificate obtained without giving a minor legal heir proper notice and representation is vulnerable to being set aside years later, however long it has stood — anyone relying on such a certificate to access a deceased person's funds or benefits should confirm all legal heirs, including minors, were properly represented before the certificate issued.

case_name: Sarabjit Kaur v. State of Punjab
holding_summary: A US-based NRI property owner alleged that imposters had been produced to pose as the actual owners in order to execute a sale of her Jalandhar property for Rs. 33 lakh, with an Economic Offences Wing investigation confirming that false persons had been presented in place of the real owners at registration. Justice Mandeep Pannu of the Punjab and Haryana High Court refused anticipatory bail to the accused, holding that the allegations disclosed a deliberate and calculated act of fraud and forgery causing substantial loss to the complainant, and reaffirmed, following the Supreme Court's ruling in Suraj Lamp & Industries v. State of Haryana, that a power of attorney is not itself an instrument of transfer of title in immovable property.
why_it_matters: NRIs who cannot personally supervise their India-based property are a recurring target for impersonation fraud at the registration stage — the ruling both signals that courts will treat such fraud seriously at the bail stage and reinforces that any sale executed on the strength of a power of attorney alone, without a proper registered conveyance, does not itself transfer title.
